Philippe Van Cauteren appointed curator of Art Encounters Biennial 2027 Art Encounters Biennial 2027: May 21–July 4 Add to Calendar Art Encounters Foundation Timișoara 46C Take Ionescu Blvd. Timișoara Timis 300 124 Romania Hours: Tuesday –Saturday 12–6pm artencounters.ro Facebook / Instagram The Art Encounters Foundation in Timișoara announces its collaboration with Philippe Van Cauteren, Artistic Director of the S.M.A.K. Museum in Ghent (Belgium), as appointed curator of the 7th edition of the Art Encounters Biennial, to be held in Timișoara (Romania). The Biennial will run from May 21 to July 4 2027, opening with a three-day program from May 21–23. The appointment also marks the beginning of a long-term strategic partnership between Art Encounters and S.M.A.K., opening a new chapter in the Biennial's development. Bringing together one of Europe's leading institutions dedicated to contemporary art and one of the region's most important biennials, the collaboration is structured around artistic co-production and professional exchange, with the aim of developing a sustainable model for conceiving and delivering a contemporary art biennial today. Philippe Van Cauteren’s involvement brings to the center of the 2027 edition a curatorial vision built around dialogue with artists and critical reflection on the role of the museum and the biennial in contemporary society. "The invitation to curate the Art Encounters Biennial 2027 is a great honor. I am delighted to contribute to this vital and unique project which promotes the visibility of art and artists through dialogue and collaboration. The opportunity to contribute to the legacy of the Biennial is a chance to learn, to discover, and to share both the local identity of Timișoara, and the constellation of relations that the working process brings. I am convinced that the Art Encounters Biennial 2027 will be more than an exhibition; it will also be a platform for national and international exchanges, including with S.M.A.K., among others." – Philippe Van Cauteren Van Cauteren has led S.M.A.K. (the Museum of Contemporary Art in Ghent) for over 15 years, making it one of the European institutions that have played an active role in supporting contemporary art in recent decades. Under his direction, the museum has developed an internationally relevant collection and initiated numerous collaborations with artists, biennials, and major institutions, including participation in the Venice Biennale. His curatorial practice is recognized for its closeness to artists and its ability to connect local scenes with international cultural networks. Philippe Van Cauteren has published, among others, the book "Letters to Artists," a compilation of letters he has written to artists over the past 15 years. "For us, working with Philippe Van Cauteren and S.M.A.K. represents a partnership grounded in genuine exchange, co-production, and professional development. At the same time, his appointment highlights a curatorial approach we strongly believe in—one that allows the central importance of art in our lives to be recognized by everyone, as a vital force in both personal and collective growth." – Diana Marincu, Artistic Director of the Art Encounters Foundation The Art Encounters Biennial is the flagship project of the Art Encounters Foundation and stands at the intersection between an experimental art festival and a contemporary art biennial. It is based on extensive curatorial research, engaging in a real dialogue with the historical and socio-cultural context of Timișoara. The Biennial’s mission is to become a creative meeting point for artists, communities, institutions, and ideas. Philippe Van Cauteren is trained as an art historian and sociologist. He is the artistic director of S.M.A.K. (Museum for Contemporary Art, Ghent, Belgium). In the past decades he has made exhibitions in Brazil, Chile, Iraq, Turkey, Nepal, Belgium. He was a.o. curator of the Belgian Pavilion (2013) and Iraq Pavilion (2015) in the Venice Biennial, and curator of the first Kathmandu Triennial (2017) in Nepal. In 2027 he will be curator of the Art Encounters Biennial in Timișoara, Romania. Art Encounters Biennial 2027 is funded by the City of Timișoara through the Centre for Projects, and it's organized in partnership with S.M.A.K Ghent. https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/08/30/w.text: Movie stars, timely documentaries and awards hopefuls convene at the Venice Film Festival Ksenia Mironova, left, and Valeria Ratnikova appear in a scene from "My Undesirable Friends: Part II - Exile." Uncredited/Julia Loktev via AP August can be a dreary month for Hollywood glamour, but the Venice Film Festival is on the horizon to kick off the busy fall film festival season in style. There will be plenty of stars gracing the red carpets when the 83rd edition of the festival kicks off Wednesday on the Lido: Noel and Liam Gallagher, Robert Pattinson, Rooney Mara, George Clooney and Penélope Cruz are among those expected to attend. Some of the films may even become Oscar nominees. But the mood feels a little different this year. There will always be a spotlight for the Hollywood contingent and the awards hopefuls posing on boats and docks in designer duds. Yet, in a lineup featuring Pattinson as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen, Dakota Johnson as Marilyn Monroe, Guy Pearce as Rupert Murdoch and Clooney as, well, himself (he’s getting a lifetime achievement award, as is Ellen Burstyn), it’s possible that much of the attention will be on a man who (probably) won’t be there: Elon Musk. Docs feature Musk, Russia and Gaza Alex Gibney’s nearly four-hour documentary about the world’s richest man has been in the works for almost four years. The Oscar-winner wasn’t sure about taking it on at first, but a good friend convinced him it would be a worthy portrait of 21st-century power — and this was before the 2024 presidential campaign and DOGE. When the documentary was announced, Musk called it a “hit piece” on social media. Gibney replied, “How would you know?” In fact, Gibney told The Associated Press he started off as a kind of admirer — as well as a Tesla owner — and sincerely wanted to talk to Musk for the film. “Ultimately, he didn’t want to talk to me,” Gibney said. “But then you start, you know, digging into the facts and you follow them where they lead. And where they led, for me, was to a place that upended the myth, I would say, of Elon Musk as a kind of modern Leonardo da Vinci … I think that the news in this film is that Musk isn’t an inventor. He’s a confidence man.” The filmmakers talked to hundreds of people on and off the record to compile a sweeping picture of the Tesla and SpaceX CEO who, Gibney said, is not dissimilar to the guys at Enron or Elizabeth Holmes. He was most surprised by how many people seemed to be afraid to be on camera talking about Musk — even his admirers wanted permission first. “I thought, wow, for such a big and powerful person, that seems awfully weak,” Gibney said. But while it’s a “dark and dangerous topic,” Gibney said, the film is also a “fun ride.” The same could be said of “My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile,” in which Julia Loktev continues her sprawling portrait of independent Russian journalists after the invasion of Ukraine. “You see this group of young, very young journalists who’ve just fled their country, like, on a few hours’ notice. They had the choice of, you know, stop reporting the truth about the war, which didn’t seem like a choice at all, or go to prison, or leave the country so they can keep telling the truth,” Loktev said. “It was a question of how long do you keep following? Because this takes place over four years. And over that time, exile becomes, of course, indefinite.” Similar to the first film, Part II runs nearly six hours. But, she said, “I hear it goes by easy.” The conflict in Gaza will also take center stage in the documentary “NAZA,” a late addition to the competition, from two of the filmmakers behind the Oscar-winning “No Other Land.” Unlike last year, no large-scale protests are planned, but the group Venice4Palestine did call on the festival to “suspend all agreements with entities and institutions linked to the Israeli government.” It also asked that the Palestinian flag be flown throughout. Hollywood eyes awards in Venice Part of the intrigue of Venice is how it might play into the Oscar race — it’s usually good for a best picture nominee or two. Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine,” starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell as 1970s CIA agents, seems like a promising candidate after his last two films debuted at Venice and went on to nominations. “The Father” filmmaker Florian Zeller returns with “Bunker,” a psychological thriller with Cruz and Javier Bardem. Danny Boyle looks at a turning point in tabloid media in “Ink.” And there’s much curiosity around Lance Oppenheim’s “Primetime,” for Pattinson’s performance and for its examination of reality television culture in the early 2000s. Japanese filmmaker Hirokazu Kore-eda is also debuting “Look Back,” about two small-town girls who aspire to be manga artists. And Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong examines themes of labor and freedom through two married couples in “Possible Love.” This is also a year in which big Hollywood hasn’t needed the sheen of the international film festival. Cannes was bereft of a big blockbuster, and the industry went on to have one of its highest-earning summers ever. The reigning best picture winner, “One Battle After Another,” skipped festivals entirely. Venice might have more Hollywood films than Cannes did, but following several years in which fates might have been prematurely decided for both would-be contenders, like “After the Hunt” and “The Smashing Machine,” and blockbusters like “Joker: Folie à Deux,” it too seems a bit more muted — at least on paper. Venice fails in its pledge to women And then there is the subject of women, specifically those behind the camera. There is only one in the main competition: Danish-Egyptian director May El-Toukhy. The same thing happened in 2018, prompting the festival that year to sign a pledge to have at least half of the films in competition be directed by women by 2020, which they have yet to achieve. Adding more insult to injury is the fact that Maggie Gyllenhaal, whose first film “The Lost Daughter” won Venice’s best screenplay prize in 2021, is presiding over a jury which includes Kaouther Ben Hania, whose film “The Voice of Hind Rajab” won the Silver Lion last year when there were six female-directed films in the competition. Only seven women have won the Golden Lion, including Laura Poitras with “All the Beauty and the Bloodshed,” who is returning this year with a short film she co-directed with Rachel Lauren Mueller about U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Minneapolis. “They’re Here” is part of the Venice Open section, which also includes Gyllenhaal’s Marilyn Monroe short “Flesh Impact.” Outside of the main competition, there are also documentaries from Loktev, Barbara Kopple and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi. There are several others in the Horizons sections as well, including a short from Saoirse Ronan. Opening Venice Days on Wednesday is Hungarian filmmaker Lili Horvát’s English-language debut, “My Notes on Mars,” about a couple — Rupert Friend and Mackenzie Davis — whose marriage is in trouble when the wife, a scientist, mysteriously disappears and then reappears the day of her memorial service. “The story argues for great love,” Horvát said. “Yet it shows the eternal limits of knowing the person we are in love with.” Venice Days is an independent sidebar in which more than half the selections are by women, including several high-profile shorts from filmmakers like Mona Fastvold and Claire Denis. “It’s good to be in a progressive section,” Horvát said.

Pictured with her are tech school instructors Emily Berry, left, and Debbie LaFrance. (Nicole Carter/Staff Writer) Maddie Poland packed a bunch of professional experience into her three years in the Oxford Hills Technical School’s early childhood development program. College looks like it will be just as challenging for the tech school’s 2026 Student of the Year. She is set to head to Husson University in Bangor for a dual degree program, and plans to stay there until she has undergraduate degrees in psychology and science and a doctorate in occupational therapy. Poland discovered her passion for special needs as a high school junior. “In my second year in early childhood we got to do internships,” she said, “and I chose my first internship to be in a resource room, working in special ed. I loved it. “Then my second placement was in a third-grade classroom, which confirmed my preference for special ed,” she added. As she gained educator proficiencies through internships Poland developed supervisory and management skills through her tech school studies. During senior year she served in an assistant director’s role among her classmates, facilitating daily staff meetings and providing feedback to first-year students of early childhood development. Advertisement She also led operational tasks, which included parental communications of the 16 children in the tech school’s preschool program, and menu/nutrition planning. “Maddie is already a teacher, of both the bigs (peers) and littles (preschool students),” Early Childhood Development instructor Debbie LaFrance said. “She is responsible and dedicated, definitely just a hardworking, well-rounded student. “She knows what needs to be done. We’d love a way to keep her back as a fifth-year student!” Poland said her mother, Oxford Hills Middle School Assistant Principal Torrey Poland, has been her biggest inspiration. “When I was younger, my mother sometimes took me along to her math classes,” she said. “I just always loved watching her teach her students. And when I saw the tech school has early childhood program, I knew that’s where I wanted to go.” She said her mind was set on special education after speaking with her mother, LaFrance and tech school instructor Emily Berry. “I feel a calling to help children with special needs,” she said. Husson University has the educational setting and programs that can propel Poland to a doctorate degree and career as an occupational therapist, making life better for children with medical conditions like cerebral palsy, she said. “It’s therapy with very specialized instruction and care,” Poland said. “I’m ready for it!” Supporting Sponsor for the Advertiser Democrat Keeping communities informed by supporting local news. norwaysavings.bank Nicole Carter Staff Writer Nicole joined Sun Journal’s Western Maine Weeklies group in 2019 as a staff writer for the Franklin Journal and Livermore Falls Advertiser.
